newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flynn slams cigarette price war. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Flynn slams cigarette price war. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn on Friday renewed his attack on the tobacco industry, calling the escalating cigarette price war a cynical ploy to lure new smokers in the face of publicity bans.

"This is a cynical attempt by the tobacco companies to recruit new smokers, which also reflects the increasing constraint on other marketing strategies," Flynn said in a statement to mark annual World No-Tobacco Day on May 31.
Flynn said he was "very concerned about the strategy of some tobacco companies who have launched price reduction campaigns". (Corrects to make clear Flynn did not name specific companies).

Rival tobacco companies are expected to follow suit because of this offensive and because of a squeeze on advertising which has seen cigarette firms increasingly resorting to price cuts, promotions, direct-marketing campaigns and prize draws to keep their top selling brands in the public eye.
Flynn hailed plans by Britain's new Labour government for a national ban on tobacco ads and sponsorship of sports events.
Britain's announcement has raised Commission hopes of getting a total EU-wide ban on cigarette ads, after five years of resistance from a blocking minority of EU governments.
Flynn is to put the issue to EU health ministers on June 5.
The Commissioner's criticism of the price war is his fourth direct attack on the tobacco companies in the last two years.

In May 1995 a blazing row erupted between the Irish commissioner and Philip Morris after a newspaper advert by the cigarette company declared that smoking bans infringed personal liberty and the European Union had copious laws telling people where and when they could smoke.
Flynn retorted that there was "no legislation of this kind", adding: "It is a pity that Philip Morris' marketing expertise is not matched by its knowledge of Community legislation.

"Similarly, the company's concern for personal liberty would have a more genuine and credible ring if it was accompanied by an equal concern for the health and lives of those people suffering from the harmful effects of tobacco consumption."

Five months later, another EU-wide Philip Morris advertising campaign inferring that measures requiring smokers to respect the rights of non-smokers were unreasonable, had the Commissioner fuming again.
"When a person choses to smoke, they are not only harming their own health but also the health of other people who are exposed to their smoking," Flynn said in a statement.

Thirty percent of all cancers were tobacco related, smoking caused three million deaths per year worldwide and six major studies had concluded passive smoking increased the risk of lung cancer, heart disease and childhood asthma, Flynn said.

The running battle flared up again last June when Philip Morris launched a major advertising campaign saying scientific evidence showed that exposure to second-hand smoke was less dangerous than drinking whole milk or eating biscuits.

"The public should greet this message with the scorn it deserves," Flynn stormed, saying the campaign was "evidence of panic in the tobacco industry about the threat posed to tobacco sales by concerns over passive smoking".
The Irishman has also crossed swords with colleagues and EU ministers over the tobacco industry.

Last December he lashed out at Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler for refusing to end EU subsidies for tobacco production which directly and indirectly provides 200,000 jobs, calling smoking the biggest single preventable cause of death in the EU.
